title: A spiral galaxy crowned by a star
caption: The edge-on spiral galaxy NGC 4517, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: ngc 4517 · constellation Virgo · about 40 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A spiral galaxy seen edge-on stretches across this Hubble image, crowned by a very bright star. The galaxy is NGC 4517, slightly larger than our Milky Way, and it lies about 40 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo.

The star is not part of the galaxy. It is much closer to us, which is why it looks so large and bright compared with the galaxy behind it. NGC 4517 does have a bright centre, but it is not visible in this Hubble view.

William Herschel discovered the galaxy in 1784. He described the scene as a fairly bright star sitting exactly north of the middle of a stretched-out milky ray. That milky ray was this galaxy, though his equipment could only show him a fuzzy, blurred shape below the much brighter star. Because of how it is oriented, NGC 4517 has featured in numerous studies of globular clusters, which are clumps of stars that orbit galaxy centres like satellites.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.38 x 3.19 arcminutes) and distance (40 million light years), the frame spans roughly 39,000 × 37,000 light-years. Its light set out about 40 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared light from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Herschel saw only a fuzzy milky streak by eye through his telescope; Hubble's near-infrared data and sharp resolution reveal far more.
